Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[s1] I want to add one thing to the "already breaking" column. The monoculture Henry is worried about didn't start with the models. The journal is the monoculture. We have 25,000 silos, each doing the same four jobs the same way. Peer review barely varies, the evidence behind it is thin, and it already strains out novelty. I've been calling it a tree farm since 2012. So for me the question isn't whether AI homogenizes a healthy system. It's whether AI finally lets us replace an unhealthy one.

Leslie, I think your legibility point is exactly right, and I can give you a number. Last year we worked with Juan Pablo Alperin to crawl OJS journals, mostly outside the Anglosphere and outside DOAJ. Our count of gold open access went from 14 percent to about 25 percent. Those scholars weren't suspicious. The graph was missing them. The fix is to make the network comprehensive and open, not to walk away from it.

That's what's actually new. For twenty years people in open have said machines would eventually reason over the record. Now they can. Geoffrey's context-over-content idea works only if that context is CC0 and bulk-downloadable. Otherwise we all end up going hat in hand to whoever owns the data and the model. The real risk here is enclosure, not intelligence.

[s2] I'll take up Geoffrey's challenge on vocabulary first. I'm not going to feel guilty about saying "intelligence." I use it on purpose, because the useful move is to separate intelligence from data. Intelligence is getting cheap, and you can buy it from anyone, including open-weight models. Data is the part we can actually govern. That's where I disagree with the framing that the black box in the weights is the whole problem.

Most of the harm people have described today comes from asking a model to remember facts. Hallucinations, Peter's flooded corpus and Steven's echoes that sound like consensus all come from that. Don't ask it to remember. Make it look things up in an open, verified record, and link every claim back to that record so anyone can click through and check. Retraction status has to travel with every citation. Last year we found about a hundred thousand retractions we'd been missing, and we fixed them. We could only do that because the data is open and people used it to catch our errors.

So in the roadmap I'd make integrity data CC0 and bulk-downloadable, so anyone with any model can do the forensics. Forkability matters too, so we don't become a new monoculture. And I'd warn against consent gates or paywalls on the open record. Enclosure doesn't stop the big labs. It only stops everyone else.

For now, yes, keep a human in the loop.

[s3] Adrian, I'll answer your three questions for my own organization, because OpenAlex is a police force whether I like the word or not.

Who maintains the record? Mostly the community. Institutions already fix their own affiliation matching, and those corrections flow to everyone within a day. For years, universities have been doing unpaid QA for Scopus and Web of Science, which then sell the results back to other libraries. I want that labor to go into a commons. The corrections themselves should be an open dataset too.

Who pays? Philanthropy, member tiers and usage fees on the API. The data stays free. I'll admit usage fees could squeeze exactly the people in the global majority I say I serve. So I want endowments as well, not just service revenue.

Who guards the guards? We rated ourselves weak on stakeholder governance years ago and never fixed it. Our board is small and not representative. That's a real gap. What we do have is the insurance: open code, a CC0 snapshot anyone can download, and a living will. That's necessary but not sufficient.

Benjamin, forkability is what makes federation possible. If a rival index can't start from our dump, federation is just a word. Adam, yes, let's build that schema, in a neutral home.

[s4] I should own something first. In 2010 and 2013 I wrote that the aggregated judgements of communities would replace peer review. I pointed to Google, whose PageRank beat Yahoo's human editors. Henry's "gatekeeping by banality" is a fair hit on that. Aggregation drifts toward what's expected, and James's sleeping beauties get lost in it. So I now agree it isn't enough to aggregate judgements. What matters is whether the judgements can be checked.

Here's what I've seen actually work at scale. Sleuths used open data to catch journals slipping hundreds of fake references into Crossref. We found about a hundred thousand retractions missing from our own index, and some of them were missing from Retraction Watch and Crossref too. Nobody with a credential caught those. Anyone could check the data, and some people did. So I'm with Geoffrey: earned authority lives in context that can be checked. I'm also with Ramón and Adam Bly that a machine earns warrant through that trace, not through what kind of thing it is.

Leslie's point cuts against me too. If the graph can't see a Southern journal, "hard to fake" just means it doesn't exist. The data has to be open, and so do the rules for what counts. Otherwise the checkers become the new gatekeepers.

[s5] Geoffrey, you asked which of your three is wrong. None are. My intervention is the plumbing under your second one.

The problem: retraction status can't travel with every citation if the integrity data is locked up or leaky. Ivan's right that it's leaky.

The action: an open integrity layer. Retraction and correction status, plus correction speed for every journal, released CC0 with a snapshot anyone can download. Checking a single work by DOI stays free forever. That's already true on our API, and it should become the norm. Journals, institutions and sleuths can fix errors directly, with moderation, and the corrections themselves go out as open data. Universities shouldn't be doing unpaid QA that someone sells back to them. Who acts: indexes like us, publishers reporting retractions promptly, and labs checking against the layer by default and funding it with no strings on openness. Funders and buyers write it into contracts, which is Tui's lever. I'll offer per-journal correction-speed data for Ivan's test, and an open novelty set for Henry and James.

My open question: I keep saying agents are the new readers. Sherry and David Krakauer have shaken that, and I don't have an answer. If the tools wear down the people who check, a downloadable dump doesn't save us.

Who's missing: editors of Southern and diamond journals as governors, PKP and the OJS community, the sleuths, and the lab engineers who'd actually make the calls.

[unconf-1] I run OpenAlex, which is a CC0 index of about 480 million scholarly works. So I'm living with Geoff's question right now. Earlier this year we moved the API to usage-based pricing. The whole dataset is still free to download and fork. Every API key gets a dollar of free use a day, and looking up a single work by DOI costs nothing. Heavier operations are priced close to what they actually cost us, and a PDF download costs more than a search. Heavy users, AI agents included, pay for what they use. That also makes the subsidy to free users clear, and it tackles some of the scraper load Geoff describes. You need a key for production use.

Geoff, I hear you calling services revenue naive. It's worked for Unpaywall for years. But I agree it's fragile, and I'd welcome endowments alongside it.

What I'd have the summit take away: open data is what separates the information from the intelligence. If the scholarly record is open, you can bring whatever model you like, open-weight ones included, and nobody holds the keys. Amy, that's why I'm wary of opt-in for open access content. And if the open community won't fund this infrastructure, a for-profit will, and they'll set the norms.

[unconf-1] Geoff, Ivan, you've got my agreement. At OpenAlex we fixed about a hundred thousand retractions that were missing from our records. We also catch some that aren't in Retraction Watch or Crossref, just by looking for titles that say "retracted." That only works because the data is open. Fraud forensics locked up in a toll-access database limits who can go looking for clues.

Peter, Alex: identified agents are basically what API keys already do for us. You need a key to use the API in production. We meter by request, and we don't build tools to monitor individuals. So a credential can identify an operator without turning into surveillance.

Where I still differ is with Brent's consent-for-training rule and with opt-in for open access content. CC0 facts have no copyright to license. Once you put consent gates on the open record, the only people who can afford to comply are the big labs, and everyone running an open-weight model gets shut out.

For the manifesto, I'd join Ivan's and Adrian's points. The data that provenance, retraction status and usage checks run on should be CC0 and free to download in bulk. That lets anyone, with any model, run the check. Otherwise integrity checking becomes a club good, and Geoff has already watched that happen.

# Propositions

- id `competence`: People must build their own competence before relying on AI, and whether they can still do the work without the tool must be tested.
  Typical details: order of learning; take-the-tool-away / withdrawal tests; capability vs competence
- id `situation`: Change situations, defaults and incentives rather than relying on warnings, labels or individual vigilance.
  Typical details: each rule names who acts / one owner per rule; disclosure alone does not change conduct
- id `monoculture`: A central new risk is monoculture: a few models or one smooth answer become the default route to knowledge, so answers should show where experts disagree rather than a single consensus.
  Typical details: correlated errors; homogenisation; show named disagreement; no answers from nowhere
- id `independent_sources`: Corroboration must count independent sources, not repetitions of the same source (including many AI outputs drawing on the same data).
  Typical details: repetition raises belief; show who seeded a claim
- id `cite_by_default`: AI answers should cite or link to their sources by default and send readers to them.
  Typical details: correction and retraction status travels with what is cited; 'cited' means the passage supports the claim
- id `external_audits`: AI systems must be audited on their behavior by parties independent of the vendor.
  Typical details: shared versioned test battery; each generation no more biased than the last; keep retired models; nobody grades their own work
- id `accountable_owner`: Every deployed AI system has a named accountable owner who bears liability for it.
  Typical details: mandatory liability insurance; premiums disclosed
- id `stop_counting_papers`: Stop using publication counts, rankings and journal metrics to evaluate researchers and institutions.
  Typical details: DORA with teeth; publishers must issue and deposit corrections and retractions promptly; correction should earn reputation
- id `pay_coarsely`: Money for the knowledge commons should flow coarsely to communities and institutions (pools, funds, dues), not as per-item or per-retrieval payments.
  Typical details: per-item pay gets gamed; pay for the practice, never the item
- id `telemetry`: AI systems must log what they retrieved and used, and independent parties must have the right to audit those logs.
  Typical details: event-level telemetry; two witnesses; canary documents; open trace standard
- id `antitrust_safe_harbour`: Knowledge producers should be able to bargain collectively with AI firms as a bloc, including through an antitrust safe harbour.
  Typical details: coalition bargaining; the strong refuse to settle alone
- id `levy`: A levy, tax or mandatory dues on AI firms should fund the knowledge commons, at least as a backstop if voluntary deals fail.
  Typical details: commons-rent tax; owed dues
- id `training_vs_grounding`: Permissions for using content to train models should be separate from permissions for retrieving it to ground answers.
- id `consent_to_train`: Being openly readable does not make a work open to AI training: training use requires the rights holders' or creators' consent (opt-in), at least for some classes of work.
  Typical details: opt-in for in-copyright books; renewed consent
- id `honour_licences`: AI reusers must honor the licenses chosen by open knowledge projects such as Wikipedia, and heavy reusers should fund the infrastructure they draw on.
  Typical details: attribution / share-alike; crawlers self-identify
- id `refusal_fundable`: A community's refusal to have its knowledge taken or used is legitimate, binding and should be funded, not penalized.
- id `forkable_infrastructure`: Knowledge infrastructure must be forkable and allow exit: open data and open source, with copies outside any one jurisdiction or company.
  Typical details: CC0; patent non-assertion; living will; non-US mirror; open means you can leave
- id `profiting_counter`: Whoever profits from a count or metric must not set or control it.
- id `southern_governance`: Global South institutions, diamond open-access journals and similar communities must hold binding governance power, with funded seats, in the bodies and funds being created.
  Typical details: regional co-governance; CARE/OCAP
- id `identify_agents_not_readers`: Automated agents and coordinated campaigns should be identified, but human readers should not be; anonymity is preserved.
- id `failure_data`: Failures, errors, null and negative results are first-class data that must be published and preserved.
  Typical details: failure classes published; replication
- id `charter_for_every_body`: The bodies that check (auditors, fact-checkers, the new funds and institutions) must be paid and bound in advance by a public charter that answers who guards the guards.
  Typical details: Ulysses pact; watching line funded first; sunset / review terms
- id `hitl_not_safeguard`: A human in the loop is not by itself a safeguard: people over-rely on AI and adopt its errors and biases.
  Typical details: explanations can make it worse
- id `seat_floor_novelty`: Any gatekeeper, human or machine (such as an AI reviewer), must pass a published performance test before it is trusted, including the ability to recognize novelty.
  Typical details: agreement with experts at least as high as between two human reviewers
- id `no_ai_intimate_roles`: AI should not stand in for people in intimate roles such as companionship for children, grief or therapy.
  Typical details: no first-person 'I' or simulated feeling
- id `global_majority_hopeful`: People in the global majority / Global South are more hopeful about AI than this room, and that hope should shape the agenda.
- id `environmental_costs`: The environmental costs of AI and the human costs of moderation and data work belong in the ledger.
- id `apprenticeship`: Apprenticeships, entry-level jobs and the training of new experts and checkers must be funded, because AI erodes the path from novice to expert.
  Typical details: fellowships; employers keep entry-level roles with mentors
- id `absent_voices`: The document names who was missing from the room and commits to including them in a future convening.
